This is a private complaint filed by the complainant against the accused for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
2. The factual matrix of the complainant's case are as under;
The complainant and accused are known to each other from past several years.
In the month of August 2021 accused approached the complainant seeking financial assistance of Rs.3,00,000/- to meet his urgent legal necessities.
Considering the request of the accused, JUDGMENT -3- C.C.3149/2022 complainant paid an amount of Rs.2,74,000/- on 01.08.2021 and accused promised to repay the same within a period of one month.

After completion of one month complainant demanded the accused to repay the same, for which accused had issued two cheques bearing No.170716 for Rs.24,000/- dated 09.09.2021 and another cheque bearing No.115536 for Rs.2,50,000/- dated 30.09.2021 drawn on Indian Bank, Cubbonpet Branch, Bengaluru in favour of complainant.
On presentation of the said cheques for encashment through his banker, the same were dishonored for the reason of "Funds Insufficient" in the account of the accused and Banker had issued memo.
The complainant has got issued legal notice through his counsel on 19.10.2021 calling upon the accused to repay the amount within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice.
The said notice was duly served on the accused.
Inspite of that accused has failed to pay the cheques amount.
Hence, the complainant has filed this present complaint.
3. In order to prove the case of the complainant, complainant got examined himself as PW.1 and got marked JUDGMENT -4- C.C.3149/2022 Ex.P1 to Ex.P8.
This court after taking cognizance of the offence issued summons to the accused.
4. In pursuance of the summons, the accused has appeared through his counsel and he has got enlarged on bail.
The sum and substance of the accusation has been read over to the accused and he has denied the same and not pleaded guilty and submitted that he has defence to make.

sentences.text: The section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, has been enacted to lend credibility to financial transactions, more particularly to negotiable instruments.
The main ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are:-
The Explanation appended to the Section provides that, the "debt or other liability" for the purpose of this Section means a legally enforceable debt or other liability.

Apart from this, Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act lays down a presumption in favour of the holder of cheque in the following terms:-
"It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that:-
The holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Sec. 138, for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability".

Also, Sec. 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act states;
"Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:-
(a) That every Negotiable Instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument, when it has been JUDGMENT -8- C.C.3149/2022 accepted,
indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration."
Perusal of records it discloses that, the complainant has followed the procedure and time lines fixed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act from the date of dishonour of cheque till presentation of private complaint.
There is no procedural lapse on the part of complainant.

23. It is the case of the accused that, he has not filled the Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques and the complainant himself filled the cheque by misusing them.

As per Section 20 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881, Where a one person signs and delivers to another a paper stamped in accordance with the law relating to negotiable instruments then in force in India, and either wholly blank or having written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument, he thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete as the case may be upon it a negotiable instrument, for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp.
The person so signing shall be liable upon such JUDGMENT - 19 - C.C.3149/2022 instrument, in the capacity in which he assigned the same to any holder in due course for such amount.

In the present case on hand, if defence taken by the accused is admitted as true for the sake of argument,
as accused was issued the blank cheque, then also the accused by handing over the signed cheque to the complainant thereby he has given the authority to fill the same.

24. For that, complainant counsel relied the Judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court reported in (2021)
5 SCC 283 (Kalamani Tex and another V/s. P. Balasubramanian.

In the said Judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court held, at Para No.13 while discussing the provisions of section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that:
"the statue mandates that once the signature of an accused on the cheque is established, then these "reverse onus" clauses become operative.

In such a situation,
the obligation shifts upon the accused to discharge the presumption imposed upon him."

In the said Judgment, the Hon'ble Apex Court at Para No.17 has held that, "even if the arguments raised by the appellants are taken at face value that only a JUDGMENT - 20 - C.C.3149/2022 blank cheque and signed blank stamp papers were given to the respondent, yet the statutory presumption cannot be obliterated, because, legally, even a blank cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act."
Further, I relied the Judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court reported in (2022) 7 SCR. 72 between Oriental Bank of Commerce V/s. Prabodh Kumar Tewari wherein, it is held that at Para-17:
"For such a determination, the fact that the details in the cheque have been filled up not by the drawer, but by some other person would be immaterial.

Even if the details in the cheque have not been filled up by drawer but by another person, this is not relevant to the defense whether cheque was issued towards payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability."

Hence, the above ratio laid down in the above quoted Judgments are applicable to the present case on hand.

Further, I relied the Judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court reported in (2023) 10 SCC 148 in Crl.
Appeal No. of 2023 (@ SLP (Crl.) No.12802 of 2022 (Rajesh Jain V/s. Ajay Singh), wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that:
"54. Nothing significant has been elicited in the cross-examination of complainant to raise any suspicion in the case set up by the complainant.
Other than some minor inconsistencies, the case of the complainant has been consistent throughout as can be noticed from a perusal of the complainant, demand notice and affidavit evidence.

In fact, the signature on the cheque having not been disputed, and the presumption under Section 118 and 139 having taken effect, the complainant's case stood satisfied every ingredient necessary for sustaining a conviction under Section 138.
the case of the defense was limited only to the issue as to whether the cheque had been issued in discharge of a debt/liability.
The accused having miserably failed to discharge his evidential burden, that fact will have to be taken to be proved by force of the presumption, without requiring anything more from the complainant.
55. As rightly contended by the appellant, there is a fundamental flaw in the way both the Courts below have proceeded to appreciate the evidence on record.
Once the presumption under Section 139 was given effect to, the Courts ought to have proceeded on the premise that the cheque was, indeed, issued in discharge of a debt/liability.
The entire focus would then necessarily have to shift on the case set up by the accused, since the activation of the presumption has the effect of shifting the evidential burden on the accused.
The nature of inquiry would then be to see whether the accused has discharged his onus of rebutting the presumption.

If he fails to do so,
the Court can straightaway proceed to convict him, subject to satisfaction of the other ingredients of Section 138.

If the Court finds that the evidential burden placed on the accused has been discharged, JUDGMENT - 22 - C.C.3149/2022 the complainant would be expected to prove the said fact independently, without taking aid of the presumption.

The Court would then take an overall view based on the evidence on record and decide accordingly."
26.
If really complainant has misused the Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques of the accused, the accused ought to have take the necessary legal action for preventing the further proceedings of this case.
The accused has not furnished any documents to show that he has initiated the necessary legal action against the complainant.
Only on the basis of accused has given reply notice is not sufficient to hold that the complainant has misused the cheques and filed the false case.

28. In the light of the above quoted Judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court of India and considering the facts and circumstances of this case, I am of the opinion that, the complainant has discharged the initial burden lies on him.
Hence, the presumption available under Section 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 is extended in favour of the complainant.
On the other hand, the accused has not able to raise probable defence in the present case.
The accused has taken defence before this court that, he has obtained the loan from one Harish and Harish has given the two cheques to the present complainant.

But the said contention has been not proved by the accused with reliable evidence and the entire evidence of the accused is not inspire the confidence of this court to disbelieve the case of complainant.
Accordingly, in the light of scheme of JUDGMENT - 24 - C.C.3149/2022 Negotiable Instrument Act, presumption exists in favour of the complainant.
The statutory presumption cannot be rebutted in such a casual manner.
There must be something concrete on the record to rebut the same.
The accused has failed to rebut the onus put on him by virtue of presumption enshrined in Section 118 and 139 of NI Act.
Accordingly, I answer Point No.1 in the AFFIRMATIVE.
29. POINT NO.2:-

There is no procedural lapse on the part of complainant.
It is the specific case of the complainant is that, the complainant and accused are known to each other.
Hence, complainant filed this case and prays for conviction of the accused.
The court can draw the presumption available under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act in favour of the complainant.
The said presumption is rebuttable presumption, if once the complainant has proves initial burden lies on him, the accused ought to have rebut the case of the complainant by adducing or producing cogent, relevant and reliable evidence.
The accused has to rebut the case of the complainant with preponderance of probabilities, if the accused has rebut the case of the complainant on preponderance of probabilities, then the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his case, the same has been held in the case of Basalingappa V/s.
Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418 the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has summarized the principles on Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
JUDGMENT - 10 - C.C.3149/2022 12.
When the burden is on the accused to rebut the presumption available under Section 139 of Negotiable Instrument Act, he is required to take up a specific defence.
But the evidence of the accused discloses that, he is taking inconsistent defence regarding denial of transaction.
21. On the basis of oral as well as documentary evidence furnished by both the parties, I am of the opinion that, for repayment of the hand loan to the complainant, the accused has issued the Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques in favour of complainant.

If really complainant has misused the Ex.P.1 and Ex.P.3 cheques of the accused, the accused ought to have take the necessary legal action for preventing the further proceedings of this case.
The accused has not furnished any documents to show that he has initiated the necessary legal action against the complainant.

has filed another case against the accused, but accused has not furnished any documents to show that, Harish has filed another case against accused or wife of accused by misusing the cheque given for the purpose of security.
Hence, the presumption available under Section 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 is extended in favour of the complainant.
But the said contention has been not proved by the accused with reliable evidence and the entire evidence of the accused is not inspire the confidence of this court to disbelieve the case of complainant.
The statutory presumption cannot be rebutted in such a casual manner.
The accused has failed to rebut the onus put on him by virtue of presumption enshrined in Section 118 and 139 of NI Act.
